Mr. Speaker, it may be of assistance to the house to have a brief statement on the revised estimates for 1968-69 which have just been placed on the table. The original estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1969 were tabled during the last session of parliament. However, their consideration was not completed during that session, so that estimates for the current year must be introduced during this session.
Last March the then minister of finance gave an undertaking to the house to reduce expenditures for 1968-69 by $75 million and to table a revised schedule of estimates. The revised estimates just tabled reflect reductions of some $80 million in controllable programs for which funds have to be voted annually by parliament. These reductions are shown by department and agency on columns 2 of pages 6A and 6C of the revised blue book.
Certain other developments which have occurred since March have made it necessary and desirable to amend further the original estimates. On July 12 last the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced certain transfers of functions among ministers. These changes are also reflected in the revised estimates; and departments and agencies have been grouped under the minister responsible for them.
The passage of time since last winter, when the original estimates for 1968-69 were prepared, has made it possible to up-date and refine expenditure forecasts for statutory programs which are traditionally shown in the
blue book, but for which funds do not have to be voted annually. In addition, we have included in the revision expenditure estimates for two statutory items which do not appear in the original estimates. I should like to emphasize that, with respect to all these statutory items, parliament has already appropriated the necessary funds in the substantive legislation which authorized these expenditures.
For most of these statutory programs, payments by the federal government are determined by a number of factors defined in the legislation itself and the government has no choice but to make the payments called for, unless parliament decides to modify the legislation. For instance, payments to provinces under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, under the Canada Assistance Plan and for post secondary education depend upon the level of expenditures incurred by the provinces which the federal government must then match.
In order to present to parliament up to date estimates of total budgetary expenditures for 1968-69, a number of statutory items-identified on page 6C of the blue book-have been revised upwards by $433 million in total. I should add that the increases in the three programs I have just mentioned account for some $229 million of the total. Another $67 million of the total increase is attributable to additional public debt charges, and the inclusion-for the first time this year-of statutory expenditures for medicare and last June's general election account for a further $49 million.
Finally, we have included in the revision the following essential requirements, totalling $33 million, for which parliament will be asked to appropriate funds. An additional amount to cover the anticipated operating loss of the Farm Credit Corporation during 196869 of $1,400,000; payments to the United States mint for coin production to meet the high demand for coinage, $210,000; additional provision for the Treasury Board contingencies vote for anticipated public service salary adjustments arising out of collective bargaining, $25 million; an addition to the original provision for the government's share of the premiums for the group surgical-medical

STATEMENT RESPECTING ATTENDANCE OF MINISTERS DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
I should like to make a statement in connection with the attendance of ministers in the House of Commons during question period. It has been the practice in the Canadian House
September 25. 1968

of Commons for as many ministers as possible to attend daily at that time. The desirability of continuing this practice has been questioned. For example, the special committee of the House of Commons on procedure of the house stated in its fourth report:
We believe that a minister ought to have more to do than to sit in the chamber each day just in case a question may come his way.
The problems of government today require in the national interest that ministers have more time to devote to departmental business than is now available during the day. In an attempt to provide extra time to ministers, a change was made last spring in the system whereby the cabinet handles its business. The cabinet committee system was restructured and regular meetings of the cabinet committees are now scheduled. This has permitted the cabinet and its committees to examine more thoroughly and expeditiously the ever-increasing number of matters before it. At the same time, the meetings of the cabinet committees have been scheduled in such a way that each minister will be free from committee attendance on certain days of the week.
I am now asking the co-operation of the house in the trial of an arrangement with respect to ministerial attendance during the daily question period. I am proposing that all ministers will attend on Wednesdays, and each minister will attend, in addition, on two other days each week. I will try to be here when orders of the day are called each day.
A roster of ministers in attendance on different days will be prepared and provided to members. It will, of necessity, remain fixed and will be subject to variation only in very exceptional circumstances. This is necessary if the ministers are to have an adequate opportunity to administer their portfolios, and if hon. members are to know each day which ministers will be in attendance.
uj commons
This is fundamental to our system. I suggest that the proposed arrangement does not conflict with that principle or with its effective operation. I do feel that the relatively small disadvantage of not having every minister in attendance every day for possible questioning on precisely that day is far outweighed by the advantage to the public interest in providing the ministers with more time to devote to administration and planning, while still being available three days out of five to answer questions.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
In closing, I want to emphasize that I am not proposing a rota system of the kind now followed at Westminster. That system works in such a way that very often only one minister answers questions on any one day after a period of notice sometimes as long as three weeks. I am asking this house, under these arrangements, to try a situation in which one half of the ministers would be here every day of the week except Wednesday, when all of them would be here. I assume that, at least for the moment, it is not the intention of the house to impose a notice requirement more stringent than what now prevails.

I fully realize the importance of members being able to question the ministers of the crown on important matters relating to the policy and actions of the government. There is no doubt in my mind about the need to keep ministers answerable to this house, or about the key role of the question period in enabling members on both sides of the chamber to make ministerial responsibility a fact of our parliamentary life.

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry and Rural Development

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to outline the plans of the government concerning its policy on subsidies to encourage industrial expansion in those areas where exceptional intervention is necessary to improve the employment situation.
As we have done regularly in the past, we have continued to check the designated areas periodically on the basis of the present criteria, in order to determine whether changes should be made.
As a result of that analysis, we added a new area to the list, namely the one which corresponds to the Levis federal manpower centre, near Quebec. Neighbouring areas of Ville Saint-George, Megantic and Montmagny have, for some time, been included in a designated area. Levis is in the same economic area, that of the Chaudiere valley, which on the whole meets the requirements for eligibility. The low level of average income for non-agricultural families is only one indication of the underemployment which exists in that area.
That is the only change made in the list of designated areas under the present rules of the program, Mr. Speaker. However, the government is considering much more important changes in the future.
The proposed changes will be implemented in two stages, since there are two acts governing the program. First of all, an area is designated according to the second part of the Department of Industry Act. However, the actual ways in which financial assistance is given to the eligible areas are set out in the Area Development Incentives Act.
The second part of the Department of Industry Act will therefore be replaced by the bill on the reorganization of the government which will, among other things, suggest the creation of a new department to take over the work of various agencies which, up until now, have dealt with different aspects of economic development.
In order to avoid uncertainty in the business world, I would like to emphasize that the government does not want reorganisation
450	COMMONS
Area Incentive Program Changes to result in the elimination of the program relating to the underdeveloped regions. As long as new legislation concerning incentives has not been introduced, those incentives will be made available throughout the regions now considered underdeveloped under the law being administered by the Department of Industry.
Furthermore, the bill concerning government reorganization that will be introduced shortly will establish the basic principles under which underdeveloped regions will be recognized. Therefore, I agree with the Prime Minister's comments on this subject a few months ago. Consequently, a region will be considered underdeveloped either because it has a low level of employment in the region concerned or because employment is low on the whole territory including that region.
This policy is much less restrictive than the one prevailing in the past. Its first results will be particularly important for the Maritime provinces. Should parliament adopt this new principle, the result will entail the admission of the three regions now under the responsibility of the Maritime provinces manpower centre that have until now, been excluded from the program. Those regions, Mr. Speaker, are Halifax, St. John (N.B.) and Fredericton. It is our intention that the incentives being offered by the development agency shall be made available to these regions, and that will be possible as soon as parliament has agreed to the government recommendations concerning reorganization.
I would like to say a few words about the second group of changes that we propose to introduce. These changes are related to the present incentive program.
The legislation governing incentives for the development of certain regions will expire on a precise date. Grants are only available for those projects which will be completed or in operation on March 31, 1971. In view of the fact that two years or more might elapse between the formulation of a project and its realization, new legislation will soon be necessary. It is the intention of the government to introduce such legislation very early next year.
That legislation will follow a serious study of the whole depressed areas incentive program. The review has already advanced far enough for me to state that it will involve significant changes. I hope that we might avoid some aspects of the program in operation, which have not been very productive

As I said earlier, it is very important not to leave the industry unaware of what is going on during the review period. That is why I wish to emphasize at this time that the government in its new legislation will propose transitional measures in order to protect the interests of corporations which are now planning to invest in the designated areas. If those corporations are eligible for incentives under the present legislation, those incentives will be made available to them and will be paid to them even though, for major reasons, the industry concerned will be able to start its production only after March 31, 1971, the deadline in the present legislation.

An area development program cannot solve the problem of unemployment. We need a greater and more general policy than that. An area program should be one which would take into consideration the potential growth of the area rather than treat an area as a charity case. As is the case now, in many instances the area development program has been a cruel hoax or promise held out to the people which did not materialize, and which did not increase their prosperity.
I hope that when the minister develops the program he will establish a new department to co-ordinate the various programs which exist now and that he will seriously consider the importance of seeking new criteria of long term growth and stability for the areas, rather than what I think is the technically faulty criterion of unemployment. subtopic: CORN-CONCURRENT ACTION TO HELP IN MARKETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I put a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) asking him whether some assistance would be given to farmers in the form of accelerated depreciation for grain storage in order to help them with storage problems, not only in the corn area of Ontario but also in the wheat area in western Canada. With regard to the second matter, regarding wheat, I did not hear him make any statement of the government's intention to assist the farmers there. We are faced with a very serious problem of grain storage in western Canada which, as has been pointed out with regard to corn, was evident six months ago. It has now been compounded by the extremely difficult harvesting conditions, and according to the latest report certain areas in western Canada may well be facing disaster for much of the harvest. I would appreciate an early statement as to the assistance which may be given with regard to storage and a clarification of the additional provision made for drying grain, because we will have a great deal of damp, tough and damaged grain, and I think we should have a statement in this regard very early.

subtopic: CORN-CONCURRENT ACTION TO HELP IN MARKETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the other members, I just took cognizance of the statement delivered by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), concerning corn in the province of Ontario.
I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary to the hon. minister (Mr. Cote) whether similar steps have been taken in cooperation with the Quebec Agriculture Department authorities in order to find a solution to the same problem existing in that province. Corn growing in the province of Quebec is increasing from year to year and the Quebec producers are obviously more and more interested in getting subsidies from the federal government, through agreement. The problem lies obviously within the federal and provincial jurisdictions and concerns agriculture in the province of Quebec. Therefore, as a representative of the farmers in the eastern area of that province, I would suggest to the Parliamentary Secretary to the hon. Minister of Agriculture, if this has not been done yet, to enter into negotiations with the province of Quebec, for the benefit of the farmers in the eastern area of that province.

subtopic: CITIZENSHIP COURT
speechtext:
I am informed by the Citizenship Branch as follows: 1. The Governor in Council may designate any court or person in any part of Canada to act as a Court for the purposes of the Canadian Citizenship Act, and any officer of the Canadian forces outside of Canada to act as a Court for the purpose of dealing with applications for citizenship made by persons serving in the armed forces of Canada outside Canada. A Court is defined in the act as meaning any superior, circuit, county or district court including in the Province of Quebec, any district magistrate as well as any court or person designated to act as a Court for the purposes of the act. In addition to courts defined by the act, 15 magistrates courts in Newfoundland have been so designated as have 56 persons across the country. Fourteen of these persons operate full time courts in 13 different locations while the remaining 42 handle cases on an occasional basis in areas remote from the normal facilities.
2. It is not possible to give the exact number of cases heard in Canada during a year because statistics are not always available on cases rejected or deferred by the courts of law. However, a very close approximation of the total number of cases heard in Canada may be given as follows: (a) 1965, 32,902; (b) 1966, 31,975; (c) 1967, 33,376.
3. All court records dealing with cases under the Canadian Citizenship Act are now forwarded to the office of the Registrar of Canadian Citizenship in Ottawa. Although this was also the practice prior to amendment of the Act in July, 1967, before that time records of applicants rejected or deferred by the normal courts of law were not so forwarded.

BIRD POPULATION IN CANADA
speechtext:
1.	Has it been established that any species of migratory or non-migratory birds native to Canada, have undergone a serious decline in population in the last twenty years in part or all of their range in Canada?
2.	If so, what are the populations most seriously affected?
3.	Have the causes of any population decline been established and, if so, what are they in some of the most serious cases?
4.	Is there any evidence that bird populations are being reduced, because their eggs are being rendered infertile by residues of DDT?
5.	Is there any evidence that any populations of Canadian birds are becoming extinct due to an accumulation of DDT in the natural food chain, as is tile case with the peregrine falcon in the Eastern United States, and with the Bermuda petrel?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: BIRD POPULATION IN CANADA
speechtext:
1. Yes. Greater prairie chicken, peregrine falcon, prairie falcon, pigeon hawk, Swainson's hawk, bald eagle, gyrfalcon and probably other birds of prey.
2.	The greater prairie chicken has now been virtually extirpated from western Canada. The Eastern race of the peregrine falcon has seriously declined.
3.	Yes. In the case of the prairie chicken, destruction of habitat is the most likely cause. For peregrine falcons, organochlorine insecticides now appear to be the most likely cause.
4.	Yes. It now appears that organochlorine insecticide residues, of which DDT residues are the commonest, are the most probable cause of the hatching failures in the recent peregrine falcon decline.
5.	The decline of the peregrine falcon in the eastern U.S. has apparently also taken place in adjacent parts of Canada, and this decline now appears to be principally due to the accumulation of organochlorine insecticide residues, including DDT, in the natural food chains of these birds.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE-PROCEDURES RESPECTING INSTRUMENTS IN VIRTUE OF STATUTES

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, September 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale):
That a special committee of twelve members, to be named at a later date, be appointed to consider and, from time to time, to report on procedures for the review by this house of instruments made in virtue of any statute of the parliament of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE-PROCEDURES RESPECTING INSTRUMENTS IN VIRTUE OF STATUTES
speechtext:
When the house rose last night, Mr. Speaker, I was dealing with this question of the appointment of a committee to examine procedures for the review of statutory instruments. At that time, I made reference to the fact that there has been a great development not only in Canada but in other countries which have given the administration the power to make delegated legislation.
The background or justification for this practice has probably never been better stated than by the Donoughmore committee in 1932-command paper 4060-and I should like to take the liberty of referring to one passage from this committee's report. It summarizes the need for delegation under four heads:
1.	Pressure upon parliamentary time is great.
2.	The subject matter of modem legislation is very often of a technical nature.
3.	If large and complex schemes of reform are to be given technical shape, it is difficult to work out the administrative machinery in time to insert in the bill all the provisions required; it is impossible to foresee all the contingencies and local conditions for which provision must eventually be made.
4.	The practice, further, is valuable because it provides for a power of constant adaptation to unknown future conditions without the necessity of amending legislation.
September 25, 1968

All these reasons may be valid, but this does not lessen the need for parliamentary scrutiny of subordinate legislation after it has been enacted and when it is in operation. I hope that the special committee which is proposed will want to ask various questions. I hope, for example, it will want to ask whether we are passing bills which authorize the minister or the council to exercise a legislative authority fully as wide as that of parliament itself. I hope it will want to ask whether the Canadian practice of having statutory instruments made chiefly by order in council rather than by ministerial regulation gives adequate ground for thinking that our instruments are less dangerous than those made, for example, in the United Kingdom. I hope the committee will want to ask whether this house ought to employ an officer to review statutory instruments in some such way as the Auditor General reviews expenditures made pursuant to parliamentary appropriation. Finally, I hope it will want to ask whether this house should set up a standing committee to scrutinize the orders and whether we should establish procedures by which both individual members and the committee could seek to have orders altered or revoked.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE-PROCEDURES RESPECTING INSTRUMENTS IN VIRTUE OF STATUTES
speechtext:
The
minister has put the matter to us in rather cold, legalistic terms. I think there is far more to this than he has indicated. I recall returning to Canada at the end of the last war. Before going to my home to resume my occupation I spent some time in Edmonton trying to refresh my memory and catch up with some of the laws which had been passed. I remember going into the court house library in Edmonton and being shown by the librarian a set of all the regulations and orders in council which had been passed during the years I had been absent. There they stood- volume after volume, shelf upon shelf and row upon row. And all these documents, intimately and deeply, had the power to impair the rights, privileges and personal position of the ordinary men and women of this country.
Later on, I recall presiding in this house over a committee established to examine the possibility of dealing with the War Measures Act. We were asked to consider what regulations might be passed and what else could be done to preserve some of the terms of that legislation. It was proposed in the course of one of these meetings that some of the regulations in connection with certain areas of discussion should be brought before the committee in order that we might form an opin-
Consideration of Procedural Changes ion before making a recommendation to this house. Mr. Speaker, we were told that if this were done so many documents would be brought that there would be no room for the committee itself to sit, so numerous were those regulations.
This is a very serious and controversial subject involving an area in which we in Canada have done nothing so far. In this respect, we are years behind other countries which have faced this problem, met the challenge and made some progress in dealing with it. My approach to this question differs from that taken by the minister. I listened to his speech yesterday and I have since reread what he said. The terms of reference contained in this resolution are, I suggest, fairly wide.
That a special committee of twelve members, to be named at a later date, be appointed to consider and, from time to time, to report on procedures for the review by this house of instruments made in virtue of any statute of the parliament of Canada.
I hold that up and compare it with what the minister said yesterday when he was giving his views as to what this committee might do, the areas into which it might go, and the areas which it should not consider. As recorded at page 438 of yesterday's Hansard he said:
One of the means of controlling administrative action to prevent interference with the rights of the individual is of course by providing legal rights of recourse, either by appeal to the regular court system or by means of prerogative writs-
I accept the first part of this. I think all of us must accept the fact that if powers have been given by a statute to any group or to any individual, whether it be the governor in council, a minister, or a person, to act, and if in addition to that right there is also given, the right to the subject who may be affected to have recourse to the courts by a method of appeal set out in the statute, and the terms of which are perfectly plain, then quite obviously this parliament should not be and must not be concerned with an issue of this kind.
But I reject out of hand the theory that because prerogative writs may be applied where natural justice is denied this means that these writs will always be applied or that we shall be free to look at these areas. These are the things this committee should be examining.
As recorded at the top of page 439 of yesterday's Hansard the minister went on to say:
This resolution and the committee to be set up will not deal with that subject matter. One of my responsibilities, as President of the Privy Council, will be to suggest further procedures-

I think this is an issue which will run collateral to the inquiries by this house.

But it is not an

speechtext: I understand that, but I do not think there should be any inhibition of this committee about contemplating this problem or the proposal of remedies merely by saying that prerogative writs do apply, or merely to say the minister has, in the terms of reference he might receive from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the right and the duty of considering other related aspects of this problem. maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE-PROCEDURES RESPECTING INSTRUMENTS IN VIRTUE OF STATUTES

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE-PROCEDURES RESPECTING INSTRUMENTS IN VIRTUE OF STATUTES
speechtext:
Good; I am glad we got that settled, Mr. Speaker. There should be the widest possible terms of reference and the widest possible consideration. I do not think there is any question about that.
Too many people have suffered injustices and inequities with no recourse as a result of delegated legislation. I recognize, all of us must recognize, that in this modern day the need to deal with the complexities of a social and economic life prohibit incorporating into a statute all of the areas of discussion, all of the proposals, all of the contingencies which might arise from time to time. We have to provide flexibility or we simply could not prepare, complete and pass a statute to meet the situation with which we are dealing. So, we have to provide that certain powers be delegated to boards, to tribunals, to corporations or to individuals, or as is most usually the case, to the governor in council.
I accept that, but in addition to any right of appeal, in areas which are not covered by appeals to the courts there has to be given to this house and to this parliament a means of making good the lack which has existed far too long of dealing with injustices and inequities which apply and which flow from these delegated legislative powers. This is what I think our committee will deal with, with the widest possible opportunity and the widest possible scope.
It may well be, Mr. Speaker, that we will decide that an ombudsman should work hand in hand with this committee. I have talked to those who occupy, and who have occupied, this position in other countries. One of the

DEBATES	September 25, 1968
difficulties which they have found is the fact that too often they operate in a vacuum. There is no means, outside of the normal realm of publicity, by which they can bring specific complaints to the legislative body in order to secure a measure of examination and investigation and a declaration by, for example, a parliamentary committee.
In addition to that, I would like to think that the committee would recommend a procedure whereby under certain conditions-and I think there will have to be criteria, there will have to be a yardstick-it will be possible to bring into this house, for discussion and consideration, a delegated authority where there has been a case of abuse; where the result of applying the authority which has been given has been to bring about something not probably contemplated or which causes injustice.
I am not suggesting that in doing this we would have to take up government time. The practice which prevails in the United Kingdom is that, by means of petition, it is possible to bring up a matter for discussion in the house, coupled with the right to move for the annulment of the offending instrument. Then, it might well be that when we come to consider this issue we will propose that with regard to certain statutes the right to pass orders in council, which is given by those statutes, should be subject to the inhibition that the orders in council should be brought back to parliament, if parliament is then sitting and, if not sitting, then within a reasonable time after parliament resumes. We might propose that these orders in council should be laid upon the table and, unless approved by this house, they would expire within a limited time.
I am not suggesting that this can be done or should be done in all statutes, but there is a strong case to be made that in certain instances the right to pass orders in council, the right to pass regulations, the right to make orders involves an area so crucial, critical and important to the liberty of the subject, that these orders in council should not be allowed to continue beyond a definite time until considered and approved by this house.
These, Mr. Speaker, are some of the areas I think we should traverse and cover. I think this is a tremendously important committee and I have great hopes that from it will flow some very beneficial results.

recalled from before, and I found it last night. It comes from the immortal Shakespeare. Possibly the minister will remember it.
But man, proud man,
Drest in a little brief authority,
Most ignorant of what he's most assured,
His glassy essence, like an angry ape,
Plays such fantastic tricks before high heaven As make the angels weep.
I refer that to the minister. He might pass it on to his colleagues and to the Prime Minister. I think it is a very useful thing to bear in mind by those who occupy temporarily the seats of the mighty.
I think this applies to civil servants and others who are given this delegated authority; good men, honest, conscientious men, but entrusted with this power they have the opportunity to cover up mistakes, to hide some inequity and injustice, to sweep their problems under the carpet. They know that at the present time there can be no right of review because if the matter is brought on to the floor of this house it is brought in such a way that it cannot be dealt with and disposed of effectively.
I think that most of those who have been given this power exercise it intelligently, honestly and equitably. However, I suggest that if it were known this power of review existed, if it were known that there would in fact be a committee of this house with the right to make the sort of inquiry I have envisaged, that would have a most salutory effect upon those who have been given this power and in their dealings with the common people, with the ordinary man, they would exercise a degree of vigilance and care which I am afraid in many instances today they do not do.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I think this is a particularly good time to bring this up. We hear talk about the just society. We heard the Prime Minister this afternoon make a unilateral declaration concerning the government's proposal with regard to the question period. As I have indicated before, I believe this is just another example of the very dangerous course which the Prime Minister and his colleagues seem determined to pursue. When I heard during the election campaign about a just society I thought it was about time the people of Canada grabbed their hats and headed for the storm cellars. The great society, the new deal, the old deal, the middle age deal, all involve a proliferation of boards, tribunals, orders,
Consideration of Procedural Changes regulations, directions and directives. Governments which come into power on an election platform based on issues of this kind operate like a yo yo; there is a lot of motion but no progress.
The statute books are filled with statutes giving rights, powers and regulatory authority to others which entitle them to deal with the fortunes and lives of the people of Canada. I venture to say, in the course of the next four years, if the people of Canada are so unfortunate as to have this government inflicted upon them for that length of time this is what we will find in the statutes which this government passes. We have the poor bewildered people of this country, the ordinary man. I believe it was Lincoln who said that God must have loved the ordinary man because he made so many of them. The ordinary man, in the general course of events today, is overpowered and overshadowed by bigness-big industry, large labour unions and big government. I suggest we will see more of this from now on.
It may well be that the better quality of life about which we hear a great deal may be improved by the passage of statutes giving government officials and the governor in council power to pass regulations, but I do not think so. I think it is about time we recognized that we have imposed upon the people of this country a bureaucratic jungle. I have no hope that we will be able to hack it down. I do hope, however, that through measures of this kind it will be possible for us at least to clear out a little space where the ordinary man can stand tall and straight again, see the blue sky, through recourse to the remedies which we hope will flow from the recommendations of a committee of this kind. We hope that he will be given the opportunity by an appeal from some of these measures to once again become an individual.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot quite copy the lyrical turn of phrase we have heard from the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin); but I have a few observations which I should like to make on this motion. We, in this party, are happy to give this motion our enthusiastic support. All members are aware of the enormous growth of delegated legislation. It is a phenomenon in this day of modern democracies. With the growing demand for legislative action, with the inevitable complexity of such legislation and the need for flexibility it is quite impossible for parliament to deal directly with the total field of legislation. Hence,
September 25, 1968

Consideration of Procedural Changes the practice of the wide delegation of legislative powers to the cabinet and other so-called subordinate bodies.
It is quite useless to bemoan this tendency, although for the past 50 years legal pundits headed by Lord Hewart, in the "New Despotism", have made it a subject for their eloquence. Although it is quite useless to bid the flood turn back, we must establish some effective review of delegated legislation if the whole democratic process of parliament is to be meaningful and not simply an empty and mocking phrase. Perhaps I might cite an example. Parliament has passed the Immigration Act which in theory lays down an immigration policy for Canada. In fact, from some knowledge, I would venture the opinion that 95 per cent of our immigration cases are dealt with by means of regulations passed by orders in council. The essential immigration policy of this country has not been subject to effective review by this house.
I, personally, am pleased that the committee, by the terms of the motion, is directed primarily to a review of action by this house in connection with subordinate legislation. There are, as members have pointed out, other forms of review such as judicial review and administrative review. Other suggestions have been made, such as the appointment of officials like ombudsmen. All of these are helpful and may even be essential. I suggest, however, that it is this house of elected members which is and should be primarily both the maker of laws affecting the people of this country and the protector of the people of this country against encroachment by the executive and its servants. Any effective steps we can take to make the supremacy of parliament more real and effective should be taken. This is essential if we are to have a fuller and more genuine democracy. We assume that the committee will be appointed, and we hope it will find useful ways for parliament to review delegated legislation. We also hope when the report of this committee is made that it will be referred promptly by the government to the house for action.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few brief remarks on that notice of motion to set up a committee to consider procedural changes. As a new member who has had however the opportunity and the advantage to attend innumerable

sittings of the house-as a visitor and secretary to the leader of the Ralliement creditiste for three years.-I have seen with my own eyes the work done in this historic chamber and its quality.
Mr. Speaker, the remarks I want to make at this stage are more of a general nature and do not deal, except occasionally, with any standing order; instead they will urge the members of that committee to pay particular attention to the spirit in which that committee should sit, in my opinion.
Mr. Speaker, the recent statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to the effect that the question period would be changed according as ministers are present or absent is, in my opinion, a breach of the fundamental parliamentary rule, in view of the setting up of this committee. I hope that the matter will be referred to that committee in due course and that report will be made to this house.
Mr. Speaker, in this parliament, we have a very important part to play, and to do so, every member should be able to exercise his fundamental rights as representative and spokesman of the people, according to the standing orders. I think that every member must make every effort so that order is maintained in the house, and a higher standard is given to this debate.
Mr. Speaker, moreover, it is my belief that Canadians truly want to be present in this house through their members whom they elected by a majority vote.
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians are present here in our discussions through the representatives they have elected, as I was saying a moment ago. All the people of Canada have a right to demand representation in the debates of the people's chamber, for it is indeed their chamber, and I feel sad about the attendance to various degrees here. I realize that members are involved on all sides in a great number of problems but the fact remains, I think, that some recommendations should be made and studied by this committee in order to assist the members so that they may fulfil their legislative and administrative roles more adequately.
As a new member and without hurting anybody's feelings, I will simply say-and I repeat it-that participation in the debates of this house has been lacking. Several members and ministers are absent. People want us to say aloud in this parliament what they are
September 25, 1968

thinking at home. I believe this governing principle should be continuously and permanently observed by each of us.
Secondly, I would like to say that I am disappointed with the many members not participating in our debates. I have, on several occasions, witnessed this situation as I have in the past three years, been listening to the debates from the gallery. Is our participation, Mr. Speaker, a matter of saving face or does it consist in contributing something to the debates? It will be the responsibility of the committee to examine this point thoroughly and ask questions.
My third comment is in connection with the quality of our discussions in this house and about the manner of our interjections. I do not claim to be better than the other members in this respect. It is a conversation between deaf persons and it has become worse since the Prime Minister has muzzled his ministers, thus preventing them from cooperating with other members.
I would therefore appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that those three comments be taken into consideration, incomplete as they may be, at the meetings of this committee, so as to improve the rules of this house and its performance.
I hope that the amendments which will be passed will improve the standard debates, encourage a thorough dialogue and an exchange of views among all parties of this house in short, that they will constantly promote a fuller co-operation from each of us.
I believe that our democracy will be lively if every member of this house is also lively. We must help the new members to integrate in their new parliamentary background and to get acquainted with the rules of the house with a view to increasing efficiency in their work.
I would like to suggest, Mr. Speaker-and I hope I abide by the rules by so doing-that lessons on parliamentary procedures be given by you, since you are an expert in this field and that I understand you teach at the University of Ottawa. Otherwise, some other capable person could give them. This would familiarize new members with the rules of the house and help them to take a more active and intelligent part in the debates.
I feel certain that many old hands in parliamentary matters would also benefit from taking those courses. An effort must be made to help the member of parliament, to revalorize his role. That is the spirit in which amendments should be made, Mr. Speaker, in

Consideration of Procedural Changes order to turn the member of parliament into a real legislator and a competent administrator.
If we are to review and modernize our rules, we should also try to give back to the members their true role, that of full participants instead of spectators who seem to wait for the Messiah.
If our standing orders, which no longer answer our present needs, are to be changed, these changes should be made in a certain spirit and according to a basic principle: rethinking and redefining the role of the member of parliament and parliament itself, and establishing the proper priorities. However, it must not be forgotten that we are here to express what the people are thinking.
I duly appreciated the most timely observations made last night by the right hon. member for Prince-Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), namely that the people must be informed of what is said and done in this historic and unique house.
In this respect, Mr. Speaker, I find it unacceptable that the Hansard should not be sent, at Her Majesty's expense, to any person requesting it. I am convinced that the hon. member for Prince-Albert will agree that Her Majesty would be pleased to allow Canadian citizens, eager to be informed, to receive this report, where the facts are not sifted out by the financiers, who would distort them, in order to keep the people in the dark and so to lead public opinion where they would like it to go.
Mr. Speaker, considering that there are about 4,000 subscribers to the Hansard, I am appalled to think that such a service is not being provided; this is one of the very serious reasons why people take no interest in the work of the house.
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to point out that the procedure should respect the role of the member, that of a representative and a spokesman. A member is a spokesman. Because of that, he must know what his constituents think. To know what they think, each member should, in my humble opinion, set up a permanent consultation system within his riding each time an important bill is put before the house.
For instance, take the famous omnibus bill which will be brought in shortly. At that time, it would certainly be opportune, in my humble opinion, or each member to hold some sort of very honest referendum in his riding, in order for him to know the opinion

Consideration of Procedural Changes of the people, and to allow a free vote to be taken, not a party vote as used to be the case with the old parties.
In short, it is a matter of bringing the people to really participate in the administration of the country. No matter what our debates are, no matter what procedure we adopt, if the Canadian people do not participate directly or indirectly in our debates, if they do not read them, we are wasting our time.
Consultation could be achieved through the mailing of circulars, letters, or through other means, in order to bring out the idea that a member is really a spokesman.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to pursue my remarks further, save for the following conclusions. I am particularly pleased that the parliament has an air of youth about it, and that it has several young members.
I am 25 years old and I am happy to sit in this parliament; a 22-year old member of the New Democratic Party, sits here also I believe. I want to congratulate him on his election and offer him my close co-operation, with a view to showing the old campaigners that young parliamentarians can do as well as their elders, provided the latter will co-operate.
Obviously, the young need the experience of the old and that is why, Mr. Speaker, I should like to appeal, at this point, to the old timers of parliament, and ask them to cooperate with us, to help us integrate. If one day they begin to feel a bit tired, we shall be here to help them. Some people have ulcers; we are in good health. Our elders have clever heads; we may have good ideas, but we lack experience.
If all those things are put together, Mr. Speaker, I think some good work can be done. But if each party refuses to come down from its ivory tower, it is useless to think that the House of Commons can engage in a lively, human and dynamic dialogue. It will be useless, because we will waste our time and end up in the best dialogue of the deaf one has ever seen.
The hon. member for Prince Albert said last night that if the debates were put on film, the end result might not be a horror movie, I say that it might be a comedy, Mr. Speaker, if things remained as they are right now.
Parliament must be dynamic to catch the interest of dynamic people. It must be serious if it wants to get the attention and the interest of serious people. It must be young to

attract even more young people. It must be efficient so that competent people from every sphere will take interest in it.
I believe in democracy as long as it is respected and lived. I want to blame this government for the way it scorns democracy by refusing to answer the questions put by the opposition, and not behaving according to a true democratic spirit. I am thinking of what took place this afternoon, with the question period confined to Wednesday and the ministers allowed to be absent.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the resolution before the house which states that a special committee of 12 members, to be named at a later date, be appointed to consider and, from time to time, to report on procedures for the review by this house of instruments made in virtue of any statute of the parliament of Canada.
I should like to commend the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), for initiating and championing the move to have this resolution placed before the house, because I consider that any effort made to regain the supremacy of parliament is a move in the right direction. I have been aware of the power of the present government of Canada, and this has worried me and many members of the house because sometimes governments which have more authority than parliament might not be as sympathetic as the democratic process would require.
I think the resolution, as stated, epitomizes the concern that in some cases instruments of government may be given unlimited power, thereby taking away some of the authority and powers which should rest with parliament.
My major reason for speaking on this resolution arises out of my particular concern as a
September 25, 1968

result of recent action taken by an instrument of government in connection with a province of Canada which I will name shortly. In trying to bring this point to the attention of parliament, permit me to quote from the legislation which cemented the union between Canada and Newfoundland in 1949. In that year when Newfoundland entered confederation, one of the terms of union agreed on by the Canadian government and Newfoundland was term 31 (a) which stated the following:
At the date of union, or as soon thereafter as practicable, Canada will take over the following services and will, as from the date of union, relieve the province of Newfoundland of the public costs incurred in respect of every service taken over, namely,... (a) the Newfoundland railway-
On April 1, 1949, by order in council the governor general in council entrusted to the Canadian National Railways the operation and management of the Newfoundland railway. The operative words of that order in council as it relates to the case are:
-Therefore, His Excellency the governor general in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Transport, is pleased to order that, effective April 1, 1949, the Newfoundland railway, including rights-of-way, wharves, dry docks and other real property, rolling stock, equipment, ships and other personal property ... the title to which is vested in His Majesty, be and they are hereby entrusted in respect of management and operation thereof to the company on the terms in the Canadian National Railways' Act expressly specified, namely, that such management and operation shall continue during the pleasure of the governor in council-
As all hon. members are aware, the terms of union and subsequent arrangements were agreed upon by the two governments, namely the government of Newfoundland and the government of Canada, both of which also agreed that the arrangement would remain in existence during the pleasure of the governor in council.
In 1966, legislation was brought in creating what is now known as the Canadian Transport Commission, and the statutes of Canada 1966-67 outline the agreements made or the legislation governing the actions and operation of the said Canadian Transport Commission. During the summer of the present year, the Canadian Transport Commission, under the chairmanship of Hon. John W. Pick-ersgill, showed exactly what powers this particular instrument of government had and also how it intended to use this power. In the summer of this year, the commission made the following decision with regard to the request of the C.N.R. to abandon the rail passenger service in Newfoundland. As we all

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), has already pointed out, we very enthusiastically welcome this motion. I hope we do not have cause to say about this motion, after it passes, what we had to say today about a motion we passed yesterday. At any rate, we feel very strongly that there is need to study the whole question of how parliament can review the legislation that is passed by bodies to which we delegate the authority to pass such legislation.
As is already clear from the debate that has taken place, various bodies are given this authority by parliament. We just had a reference

to the Canadian Transport Commission. My colleague from Greenwood referred to what happens in the field of immigration. Indeed, there are a great many boards and commissions that are given what amounts to legislative authority by acts of parliament.
I rise to speak in particular of a very important body which gets this kind of authority from parliament and which I think all too often abuses it. I refer to the cabinet itself. After all, that august body consisting of the ministers of the Crown does have the right to pass orders in council in terms laid down for them in various statutes of parliament. However, it is a very clear principle that the cabinet does not have the authority to legislate beyond the terms given to it by an act of parliament.
I want to refer to one particular case which I think demonstrates the need for this kind of review. I have made a brief reference to it already by asking a question of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner). My question was put to him on September 17, as recorded in Hansard at page 102, when I asked him about an order in council which was passed in April, based on the Financial Administration Act.
I asked him in particular if he would compare the passing of that order in council with one that was passed by the Diefenbaker government in June, 1962. I asked, to be even more specific, whether the Department of Justice had checked all aspects of this matter before giving approval to the passing of this order in council. It struck me as rather strange that when I asked about this order in council the Minister of Justice did not seem to know which one I was talking about. When he did come back with the answer a few days later, namely yesterday, he managed to give me the good old one word answer. His one word answer to my question was simply "Yes". In other words, all I have been told by the Minister of Justice is that all aspects of this matter were considered by the Department of Justice before approval was given to this order in council.
To make my point, a brief bit of history has to be given, but it is history well known to many members who are still in this House of Commons. In June, 1962, a week after the election on June 18 of that year, the government of that day passed an order in council which had the effect of raising import duties. This is something that only parliament can do; we thought everyone knew that. But the
September 25, 1968

then government ol Canada found an ingenious way by which it could raise import duties. It did it by order in council. It used the Customs Tariff to raise various categories of duties by a rather large amount, and then reduced them to the figure it wanted by applying the remission privileges contained in section 22 of the Financial Administration Act. It was ingenious, but there is no doubt in my mind that it was wrong, that it was an abuse of the power to pass legislation by order in council.
I think it is a statement of fact that I was the one who discovered it and first started asking questions about it in the House of Commons. But for the purposes of what I want to say now, the more important fact is that it was the Liberals of that day who came in for the kill. It was Hon. Paul Martin, who sat in the front bench on this side of the house, and the present Minister of Justice who sat in the back bench on this side of the house, who really went to war, who really manned the barricades, who really called for the downfall of the Conservative government because it had exercised the privilege of passing legislation by order in council, which it was the right of parliament only to do.
The government of that day, of course, told us that the Department of Justice had found that this order in council was perfectly valid, that it was properly drawn and quite legal. But a few months later, after an election had taken place, we had a change of government. In the meantime, some people were taking the government to court over this order in council because, after all, duties had been raised by a substantial amount.
So the new Liberal government got from the same Department of Justice the opposite ruling, a ruling quite contrary to the ruling that had been given to the Conservative government. The ruling then was that the order in council of June, 1962, was invalid and that there had better be legislation to validate it.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I recite that bit of history, Mr. Speaker, not to open old wounds but to place it before the house to enable us to see what is now happening. Let me repeat that in 1962 and 1963 this was a terrible abuse of the power of order in council. The Liberal government now comes along and uses the same order in council technique, the same statute-the same Financial Administration Act, section 22-to reduce duties. The order in council reads, in part, to the effect the duties will be the

The order in council, in its very language, admits that the government is doing by executive action what it had earlier thought had to be done by an act of parliament.
I see that you are on the edge of your chair, Mr. Speaker, and that it is after five o'clock, so I will continue my remarks when we return to this motion.

point of view in just three tiny areas that on the map look like three 10-cent pieces. There are, of course, countless small fishing settlements along the east coast of Labrador, but what I speak of is the fantastic industrial potential that lies inland.
I am proposing, Mr. Speaker, that this government give consideration, not only in the interest of Labrador but in the interest of the whole country, to the possibility and advisability of constructing a second trans-Canada highway to the north of the existing trans-Canada highway. This highway would join the present highway in the far west, cross Canada, go through northern Quebec, down through Labrador, across the Strait of Belle Isle, a distance of some eight or 10 miles, by means of a tunnel, bridge, causeway or what have you, and then come down through northern Newfoundland to connect with the present trans-Canada highway. In effect, this would make it a trans-Canada loop or belt, or whatever you wish to call it.
The people who live in Labrador now, in the towns of Labrador City, Wabush, Goose Bay, Happy Valley and, of course, that big power development at Churchill Falls, and in all the coastal communities are virtually prisoners. They have no access to the trans-Canada highway, or in fact to any highway. They have no access to Air Canada, except at Goose Bay perhaps once a week. The fare there is exorbitant and makes the journey completely impractical. The people have no access to the C.N.R., and it looks as though the whole province of Newfoundland will soon have no access to the C.N.R. They have no access to the C.B.C. Now and then canned programs are made available to them. I know of instances where our people have watched national hockey games in June.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Our people are Canadian in name only and are without the privileges enjoyed by other Canadians. Their pioneering spirit has received no encouragement and our up and coming generation has been given no road to follow other than the road which leads to prison. Most people say that since Newfoundland is an island, it is impossible to link it with the trans-Canada highway system. Those people forget that a large part of Labrador is also part of Newfoundland and shares a border with Quebec. Those living in Labrador are entitled to be linked by highway with the rest of the country just as people living in all other provinces are linked by highways to the
September 25, 1968
rest of the country. Such a link ought to be forged where it is physically possible to do so. Joey Smallwood's unholy fear of Quebec should not be a factor in preventing such a link.
Quebec seems to get on quite well with Ontario. You can go from Ontario to Quebec by road and from New Brunswick to Quebec by road. I do not know if the proposal of a highway link with any part of Newfoundland has been considered seriously by previous governments, but if it has been considered and if a study has been made, then I should like to see the report on that study. If such a study has not been made, then I should like to see it made. It is high time that governments forgot their preoccupation with a few of our large cities and concentrated their attention to some degree on that part of the country which holds the key to our future, the north.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the notice of motion presented by the honourable member from Newfoundland and Labrador, who represents the constituency of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Peddle) reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give immediate consideration to the advisability of constructing a second Trans-Canada Highway that would link Labrador with the rest of Canada and thus develop the greatest remaining storehouse of natural wealth in Canada.
I may say at once, Mr. Speaker, that this motion is quite natural and well meant and it is, on the part of that member, a sign of clearsightedness. I would be inclined, as a matter of principle, to second his motion, especially if the honourable member would add that this highway could cover a part of the province of Quebec: for instance, starting from the Hyppolite Lafontaine tunnel in Montreal and going through Berthier, Trois-Rivieres, Quebec, across to Tadoussac and as far as the Labrador region. As a matter of principle there is obviously no objection to that. This is a remarkable project, as was said by the honourable member, and it is an undertaking that is bound to create considerable development in one part of Canada that contains untold wealth. However, Mr. Speaker, I believe two factors must, at this time, be considered. The notice of motion introduced by the hon. member-with all due respect-
Request for Second Trans-Canada Route seems to be worded in an equivocal language. In the first place, it reads in part:
-the government should give immediate attention to the advisability of constructing a second Trans-Canada Highway-
"Immediate attention"-Mr. Speaker, in the course of the debate on the Speech from the Throne, I heard some hon. members say that the government had not done this or that, had not examined this or that, and that we do not know where we are heading with the just society. Questions are being asked as to where we are headed with the new procedure.
Therefore, the opposition seems to understand that this new government, that wants to create a new policy, already has, as regards work groups or task forces as our English friends say, a large number of organizations, and the one responsible for administration will have to work day and night for many years to come in order to get all this done. If we are going to tie them down to the consideration of a project of this scope immediately, I am under the impression, Mr. Speaker, that it will be too great an enterprise, that we are putting the cart before the horse.
After all, as my honourable friends say, one must set certain priorities. Now, there are things that have been left undone and that cannot be settled at present. Hence, it is unwise I think-and I will attempt to prove it in a few minutes-to force the government to consider this question immediately.
Secondly, the hon. member talks about the advisability of building a second Trans-Canada highway. I say that this is ambiguous Mr. Speaker. To me, a Trans-Canada highway is one that would start in British Columbia-I say this in English in order to please my friends who chide me for calling it "Colom-bie-Britannique" when I am asking them to say "Trois-Rivieres" instead of Three Rivers-and go through all the provinces up to Labrador and Newfoundland.
Well, Mr. Speaker, there is ambiguity here. To me, this would be an interprovincial highway. First, we would have to get both provinces to come to an agreement, which would not be a mean thing, Mr. Speaker. Everybody knows that since the Labrador matter has been discussed for many years now. Some people in my province say that Newfoundland robbed them of Labrador and they will not change their mind easily about that. Therefore, can one imagine how we could have them come to an agreement in order to build that interprovincial highway, with the federal

482	COMMONS
Request for Second Trans-Canada. Route government contributing its share eventually, which would bring no objection on my part, but I should remind my hon. friend that the government is already facing projects that will require almost phenomenal investments. There is, for instance, the medicare scheme, which has not been implemented yet to all practical purposes and which is going to cost, it seems, some $800 to $900 million. The provinces are reluctant to adopt this plan, as they claim they cannot afford it.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Therefore, if it is doubtful if this is really a Trans-Canada highway, and if the whole Canadian people are required to pay the cost,
I wonder whether this is very wise.
Secondly, there is the Prince Edward Island causeway where the work has been progressing slowly because of the present financial situation. There is a good deal of other projects which the government had considered and initiated such as, for instance, the C.B.C. building in Montreal the construction of which has to be postponed due to the financial situation.
Even if the project were only to be considered at the present time, it would mean considerable investments, because appraisals are always expensive. A feeling is then created in the country which is contrary to the directives of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and of the leaders who control Canadian finance. According to them, all levels of government, whether municipal, provincial or federal, should now set an example by restricting their investments, encouraging individuals to do the same, because of the uncertain financial climate which exists in the whole world and naturally also affects Canada.
Therefore, psychologically speaking, if we undertake a project needing an investment of several million dollars, we run the risk of having the Canadian public say: the federal government is irresponsible; they ask us to restrict our investments, they have put off projects already decided on, mapped out and accessed because of the existing financial problem, and yet now they are undertaking another multimillion dollar project.
Information about those things can be obtained, Mr. Speaker. In fact, I have here the annual report on the Trans-Canada highway for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1967, published by the Department of Public Works. And just to prove you, for instance, that it would be difficult for Quebec, Newfoundland and the federal government to come to an

DEBATES	September 25, 1968
agreement, it is only necessary to note that the first bill goes back to 1949, but its expiry date had to be postponed several times, that Quebec decided to participate in the project only in 1960, on several conditions and that, finally, the cost of the whole thing was $825 million, and to use an expression which is quite popular at home, $825 million it is not just peanuts.
In my opinion, this notice of motion is ambiguous, equivocal, in that it refers to a Trans-Canada highway when it is instead an interprovincial one. If my hon. friend wants to pursue his project-which I agree has a certain merit-he should see, for example, our friend the Premier of Newfoundland, suggest that he meet the Premier of Quebec, then that they clear the ground or, at least, understand each other and he should make sure that they are ready to work together, which is not too certain, and get them to decide whether they are able to pay the 50 per cent share of their required contribution or the percentage agreed upon.
That is not too sure, because they both have financial difficulties, and here, I can picture the premier of my province pulling aces out of his sleeve and saying: "You stole Labrador from us; first, give back Labrador, if you want us to talk business." If the premier does not say it, some of his ministers or other Quebecers will, and maybe Mr. Smallwood will voice his own conditions. This might be the first step; only after that could the provincial government intervene. But as far as I am concerned, it would be illogical at this moment to let the public know of the idea that the federal government would embark upon a project of that importance, even though it is worthwhile-and I repeat that it is-because all worthy projects have to be implemented step by step.
I am sure that out of the 263 members here, 200 have brilliant plans for the investment of government's money, and a thousand good reasons, but there comes a time when we must say: Well, we have to consider our means, because the bill will go to the taxpayers.
Efforts are made to reduce the budget. I saw how our friends opposite reacted this afternoon when the main estimates were mentioned. Right away someone said: Have they increased or decreased? Then, someone else said: No, they have increased but savings have been made just the same in the sense that otherwise the estimates would be much
September 25, 1968
higher. What should we think about the passing of such a notice of motion? I assess it only if it covers the province of Quebec and I made some rapid calculations. Even if it covers the province of Quebec only and the part concerned in Newfoundland and then connects with the national highway, $400 or $500 million have already been spent. Although the bill is very worthwhile, my friends will no doubt understand that, even if we would all like to drive a Cadillac or fly in a Jet Star, if we cannot afford them we do not buy them.
I come back to one of my earlier conclusions: the notice of motion as drafted is ambiguous because it is not about a Trans-Canada highway, but an interprovincial highway, which is something completely different. Furthermore, it burdens the government with an immediate responsibility, since it says that the government should give immediate consideration to it. I see, for instance, the president of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) who stays up until all hours, not to go on a spree, but to do his homework for the next day. He will be called upon to create a specialized research team, to find experts to give immediate consideration to that. He or another minister, will have to keep an eye on these studies, at a time when the idea of ministers being absent during the question period is being frowned upon. He will surely have to be absent if he is given an additional burden. He is quite busy enough as it is and the same goes for other government experts.
Then it is equivocal, premature and does not take into account the fact that the federal government has already some considerable commitments of which it must defer the carrying out, because it must precisely take into account the taxpayers' solvency. This is why the opposition is charging the government with having overburdened the taxpayers; but such a procedure which existed well before the government was in power, is obviously adjusted to the cost of living and meets all the demands of the members which lead the government to make investments even when they are beyond its means.
Now, I will summarize my comments, Mr. Speaker. The government has already undertaken to make huge investments beyond the reasonable limits which it had set. It should now honour its first commitments.
Secondly, a situation is created which runs counter to the directives emanating from the honourable Minister of Finance, since word has spread that the government is ready to
Request for Second Trans-Canada Route commit itself, without batting an eye, to a multi-million dollar project, even if it is deemed as worthy as it was said to be, a moment ago.
Thirdly, Mr. Speaker, this project is drafted in ambiguous terms, since it deals with a trans-Canada highway, whereas it should be an interprovincial highway, I think, not a trans-Canada highway. I also believe that, previous to this, an agreement should be reached between Newfoundland and Quebec, and this will not be easy. It is not necessarily for the federal government to take the first step toward such agreements. This should be done by our Newfoundland friends, the main parties in this matter. It is they who want to be in, so it is they who should start consultations with the Quebec government.
If they manage to reach a reasonable agreement, this will give the federal government time to breathe, at least for four or five years, as it will probably drag on judging by the time it took for the Transcanada highway. Now, in 4 or 5 years' time, the financial international climate will have improved-at least we hope so. Of course, the federal government's situation will have certainly improved too and it is quite possible that at that time it will be in a position to say: You made an agreement. This is an interprovincial highway. The two provinces concerned have reached an agreement and we are ready to contribute for such proportion, since it has to do with the development of natural resources in a part of the country where resources are plentiful.
Mr. Speaker, it is the reason why, whilst I recognize that in principle the proposition is worthwhile, I object to it for the reasons I have just enumerated.

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Peddle) on having introduced this motion. I admire the frankness with which he admitted that he has not considered all its implications. What he is suggesting is something very far reaching, a highway from the east to the west. Well, we have heard a similar proposal made many times, but the suggestion has always been that the highway be built from the west to the east. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) is in favour of starting this new second trans-Canada highway in northern British Columbia and heading it eastward. It is interesting to find a new member wanting to start it in the east and head it west.
