Request for Second Trans-Canada Route
The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) is probably wrong on three or four counts. One of them would be the assumption that this proposed second trans-Canada highway would go through Trois-Rivieres. I am sure we have in mind that it would be placed much further north, in which case it would not have much effect upon Trois-Rivieres.
It was interesting to hear those two hon. members speak, because obviously the one on the Liberal side is not liberal but conservative, and the one on the Conservative side is not conservative but liberal-with a small "c" and a small "1", of course. The situation is that the man who calls the tune must pay the piper, and the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres is on the side of the house which is more directly concerned with raising the money. It is probably easier to consider this proposal from the point of view of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador who would have less preoccupation with raising the necessary money than would a supporter of the government.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I believe there would be a great deal of merit to the development of a second trans-Canada highway. I know much argument was advanced against the federal government becoming involved in the building of the first trans-Canada highway. The proposal to build this highway was advanced in the early 1940's and was brought to fruition in the Trans-Canada Highway Act of 1949. The first highway was built on a voluntary basis. Any province could participate if it wished to get the benefit of the program. If it did not wish to participate it need not, and the province of Quebec stayed out until the early 1960's.
Difficulties have arisen in some provinces regarding the development of interprovincial highways. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres was correct in saying that some highway programs have already resulted in an interprovincial exchange. This is true with respect to the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec. This gives rise to my interest in this matter. In Ontario we designated the northern route of the trans-Canada highway through the northern part of the province, and highway No. 17 was designated as the southern route of the trans-Canada highway. Such a program spurs people's imagination. By building the trans-Canada highway we provided a route from east to west which now carries most of our Canadian traffic. A person from the west finds it no

DEBATES	September 25, 1968
longer advantageous to travel through the United States to get to eastern Canada. As a matter of fact, he can travel through central Canada over two different routes.
The building of the trans-Canada highway resulted in greater development of tourist industries, the profit from which is now more than the cost of building the highway. The highway was built with a 50 per cent contribution of the cost to a provincial government by the federal government, and the federal government made a 90 per cent grant of the cost covering 10 per cent of the route through a province where the most difficult construction was involved.
I am sure that if that 10 per cent link in Labrador were to take the form of a tunnel connecting Labrador to Newfoundland it would produce some interesting results. I understand that studies have been made concerning a proposal to build a causeway from Labrador to Newfoundland, and it was discovered that if a causeway were built the course of the Gulf Stream would be changed. As a result England would have a climate similar to northern Canada. It would have snow and ice for six months of the year, and most of the northern Europe would be in a semi-frigid state for four or five months of the year.
If the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador does a little research, I am sure he will find it not too difficult to raise subscriptions from European countries and Great Britain to help finance the construction of a tunnel rather than a causeway, because a tunnel would not affect their climates.
I have had the opportunity of travelling through northern Quebec. I know of the construction taking place in many of its northern areas. There is a very good highway coming from the west through Rouyn, Noranda, Val d'Or, and La Verendrye park down to Mont-Laurier. If one is travelling from west to east and wishes to come to Ottawa I recommend that highway. I think westerners should travel it at least once because it is a very interesting trip. It is not much longer than any other route although it appears to be longer. If this highway were the northern route of the trans-Canada it could be extended through the Lake St. Jean area, over to Labrador City, on into Labrador, and from there reach the island of Newfoundland.
I believe that with the advent of a second trans-Canada highway tremendous development would take place in the area through
September 25, 1968

which it runs. Almost all of the railway-development in the northern areas of B.C., Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec has been in a north to south direction. The only feasible way to provide transportation across those northern areas is by highway. If a highway were built many natural resources would be opened up for development.
It is all very well for the government to say it will not consider a second trans-Canada highway. I wonder, has it not considered some of the advantages which would flow from the building of a second trans-Canada highway. For many years I, as a Canadian, was not proud of the fact that if I had to go to western Canada I had to drive through the United States to get there. Our country was developed by the building of a railroad across it. But now modes of transportation have changed. A second trans-Canada highway is necessary.
We are plagued with unemployment, but I would not suggest that we should build highways to help combat unemployment. We would be very disgusted if we saw the federal government participate in a program of pick and shovel work to help fight unemployment.
Many rugged construction problems were solved in the building of the first trans-Canada highway. The lessons learned then, covering methods of construction and the building of a highway in winter time, could reduce the costs of a second highway. It is not easy to forecast the cost of such highway construction, nor is it easy to forecast how much resource material would be developed as a result, but I suggest that any party which wishes to implement a vision of expansion, as well as the vision of a just society for all parts of Canada, must give consideration to providing modern means of transportation in northern areas. Such a program would meet the wishes of the people living in the northern areas, and people in the rest of Canada have always shown a great deal of sympathy for the development of under developed areas.
While the hon. member who has proposed this motion has apologized for not having done a lot of research on the matter, I think the government has not done enough research. I think the hon. member is correct in his proposal for a second trans-Canada highway and for suggesting that a study be undertaken to see what it costs, and what

I think the government must have a much better answer before it can refuse the hon. member the opportunity of a study of this matter which is long overdue. I should like to congratulate the member who comes from the east for initiating a program that has long been the hope of some people from the central and western parts of Canada. I hope he is in this house long enough to see the completion of this highway, and I hope there will be a tunnel rather than a causeway. speechtext: It being six o'clock this house stands adjourned until tomorrow at 2.30 in the afternoon.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, September 26, 1968

A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting revised estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1969, was presented by Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board) and read by Mr. Speaker to the house.
